1. **The idea.** The title is "The pile that sank." It seems to show the invested "pile" of money (the renter's portfolio) falling at some point along the way. The caption reads "lowest point of each pile, one per start month," so each possible start month gets its own pile. The text says 183 of 307 of those piles dipped below $92,000. That is about 60% of them. The sources named are FHFA, BLS, Freddie Mac and K. R. French (CRSP). The "ILLUSTRATIVE" tag marks the picture as a schematic rather than exact data.

2. **What changes.** Very little changes in the first five frames. A blue band stays in place and the title and captions stay the same. In frame 5 the title is replaced by the gold line "183 of 307 dipped below $92,000." In frame 6 the blue band is replaced by rows of small 3D house models, and the title and the caption about lowest points disappear. The "ILLUSTRATIVE" tag and the "All $ in dollars of the day" label also drop out of frame 6. I can't see a clear time axis or a moving pile in these frames.

3. **What it means.** Across 307 historical start months, a renter who invests would have seen the portfolio fall below $92,000 at some point in most of them (183 of 307). Even if the investing strategy ended up ahead, the path was often rough. The $92,000 figure is probably related to the down payment, but the frames don't say so. The frames also don't say how the renter and buyer compare in the end. The footer notes that this is US-only, history rather than a forecast, and in dollars of the day. The last label could mean nominal, not inflation-adjusted, dollars, but the frames don't make that clear.

4. **Advice a viewer would take.** The frames give no explicit advice. A viewer might infer that "rent and invest the difference" carries real risk of a drawdown, and that the strategy isn't a sure win. The frames don't tell them whether to rent or buy.

5. **Source of the conclusion.** The advice in 4 is my own inference. The animation itself gave no recommendation. It only had the "history, not a forecast" disclaimer and the 183-of-307 statistic.
